strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and challenging task: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video onto a new input image/video, which is difficult to specify with text or static conditions.

Introduces a large-scale multi-source dataset construction pipeline, including LoRA-based image-to-video effects, an automated video-to-video pair generation pipeline, and programmatic code-based temporal effects, yielding over 120K triplets and 1,700 effects. This is a potentially valuable resource for future work.

Extends a modern video diffusion backbone by jointly conditioning on reference-video latents, input-video latents, text, and masks in a feed-forward manner, and demonstrates controllable inference-time guidance for balancing input and reference adherence.

Provides qualitative results and human preference studies across image-to-video, video-to-video, and code-based effects, with reported large win rates in reference adherence and some generalization to unseen LoRA effects.
The paper is generally clear about its limitations and discusses inference cost and failure cases such as occlusion and human-centric bias.
weaknesses: The title/framing as 'tuning-free' is misleading: the method fine-tunes a 14B video model with LoRA on a large curated dataset. It is optimization-free only at inference time, so the core contribution is a trained model rather than a tuning-free method.

Evaluation lacks ground-truth paired outputs. The main quantitative metrics are CLIP/VideoPrism similarities to the input or reference, which do not directly measure whether the intended temporal effect was transferred, whether content/motion was preserved, or whether reference content leaked into the output. For many validation effects, ground-truth targets could plausibly have been generated but are not evaluated.

Validation for video-to-video effects is generated by the same automated pipeline or the same families of programmatic effects and hyperparameters used for training. This creates a circularity risk: the model may learn generator-specific artifacts rather than generalizable temporal effect transfer. Claims of unseen-effect generalization are therefore only partially supported.

Baselines mostly cannot condition on a reference video and instead receive text prompts. This makes the reported advantage expected rather than compelling. The more informative 'No Ref' ablation shows only marginal mean-score gains in some settings (e.g., +0.15 in I2V), and the human-study reporting is hard to interpret because high win rates are paired with very small mean differences without confidence intervals, annotator agreement, or statistical significance tests.

VBench-style metrics do not consistently favor the proposed method; for example, dynamic degree is lower than VACE (Pose) for code-based effects, and aesthetic score is lower than VACE Depth in some video-to-video settings. The paper summarizes these as comparable without significance analysis, which weakens the empirical case.

Architectural and implementation details are insufficiently specified for reproducibility: the exact handling of reference latents, mask semantics, token merging, LoRA configuration, training schedule, dataset splits, validation filtering, and data-release/licensing details are either absent or deferred to a supplement that is not fully convincing.

No architecture ablations isolate the contribution of the reference-video conditioning design versus simply adding more conditional tokens or fine-tuning on the new data. There is also no comparison to per-effect LoRA adaptation or other reference-based customization methods, despite those being natural alternatives.

Real-world video editing is demonstrated only qualitatively. The paper claims general temporal effect transfer, including lighting and camera motion, but the quantitative evaluation is centered on synthetic or LoRA-generated effects, leaving real-video effectiveness under-supported.
Societal-impact and ethical considerations are largely absent, despite the clear potential for misuse in video manipulation and deepfake-style effect transfer.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and potentially useful problem: transferring time-varying visual effects from a reference video to a target video/image, going beyond text-only or keyframe-conditioned video editing.

It introduces a multi-source data-generation effort (LoRA I2V effects, automated V2V pipeline, programmatic effects) and reports a large number of triplets/effects, which could be valuable if properly released and validated.

The method extends a strong video diffusion backbone with joint conditioning on reference video, input video/image, and text, and inference is feed-forward rather than requiring per-effect test-time optimization.
Qualitative examples and a user study suggest the approach can produce plausible effect transfer in some cases, and the controllability discussion via guidance scales is a practical addition.
The paper includes some implementation details, a limitations section in the supplement, and promises code release, which is positive for future reproducibility if fulfilled.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is not convincing for the core claim. The strongest baselines are text-only or first-frame/pose/depth-conditioned models that cannot consume the reference effect video, so high reference-adherence win rates are largely expected and do not establish effective reference-based effect transfer.

There is no true reference-conditioned baseline or adaptation of existing reference-based video/image customization, style-transfer, or concept-personalization methods. This makes it difficult to judge whether the proposed architecture is actually necessary or better than a simpler reference-conditioning approach.

The quantitative metrics are weak proxies for the task. VideoPrism/CLIP embedding similarity to the reference can reward copying the reference content rather than transferring only its temporal effect, and there is no direct metric for effect fidelity, motion preservation, or disentanglement of effect from reference content.

The V2V training data and validation data are generated using the same or similar conditional video model family used as a baseline, creating a self-referential evaluation setup. The model may learn to distill that generator's effect behavior rather than generalize to real reference effects.

The dataset is heavily biased and limited. Many effects are human-centric LoRA transformations or simple programmatic filters/hyperparameter variations, while the paper claims broad generalization to complex temporal effects. Validation code-based effects share the same effect families as training, so generalization claims are overstated.

The user study lacks critical details and statistical rigor. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-annotator agreement, per-comparison sample sizes, or annotator demographics reported in the main paper, and the very high win rates require stronger justification.

For I2V, the user study reports only reference-video adherence, not input-image adherence, even though preserving the input first frame is essential. The CLIP first-frame similarity is actually lower than baselines, which is not adequately addressed.

The method has limited technical novelty: it mainly concatenates reference latents into an existing FLF2V/VACE-style conditioning architecture. There is no explicit mechanism to separate the reference effect from its content/motion, and no architecture ablation validates the design choices.

The architecture description is internally confusing in places, e.g., width-wise versus channel-wise concatenation and merging of repeated reference latents. The token-count and conditioning details need clearer formulation and validation.

Quantitative results are mixed or unfavorable in important places: lower first-frame similarity for I2V, lower input-video similarity than VACE-depth on neural V2V, and sometimes worse VBench aesthetic/dynamic-degree scores. The paper downplays these outcomes rather than analyzing them.

Reproducibility is questionable at this stage. Code and dataset are not yet available, LoRA effects/prompts are partially obfuscated, exact data splits and filtering are unclear, and the pipeline depends on several external generative models whose versions/settings may affect results.

Ethical and societal implications are essentially unaddressed. The dataset involves human-centric identity transformations and realistic effects, but there is no discussion of consent, licensing, misuse, or safeguards against deepfake-style applications.
The paper overclaims terms such as 'first,' 'tuning-free,' and 'new benchmark' without sufficient support. A benchmark requires standardized evaluation protocols and metrics, which are not provided.

strengths: The paper tackles a new and practically relevant task: transferring complex, time-varying visual effects from a reference video to a target image/video, which is difficult to specify with text or static conditions.

It introduces a large-scale dataset of over 120K triplets covering over 1,700 effects, built from three complementary sources: LoRA-based I2V effects, a scalable synthetic V2V generation pipeline, and programmatic temporal effects. The dataset and scalable V2V pipeline are significant contributions.

The method extends a strong video diffusion backbone to jointly condition on reference video, input video/image, and text, and performs inference in a feed-forward manner without test-time optimization per effect.

The experimental section includes qualitative comparisons, user studies, and quantitative analyses across I2V, V2V, and code-based effect settings. Results show strong human preference for reference-effect adherence and generalization to unseen effect categories.
The paper is generally well organized, with technical details, dataset construction, and implementation specifics provided; limitations are acknowledged and future work is discussed.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks fair reference-based baselines. The main comparisons are against prompt-only or condition-only models that cannot see the reference video, so large reference-adherence wins are expected; the paper does not adapt or compare against recent reference-based video editing or customization methods that could serve as more informative points of comparison.

The user-study results show some internal inconsistencies or at least require more explanation. For example, against the 'No Ref' ablation, the reference video adherence win rate is high (81.5% for I2V, 92.9% for neural V2V) while the mean score improvement is very small (+0.15 and +0.18, respectively), suggesting either many ties or a win-rate metric that is difficult to interpret. Statistical significance and annotator agreement are not reported in the main paper.

Quantitative metrics are weak proxies for effect transfer: CLIP/VideoPrism embedding similarities to reference or input videos do not directly measure whether the intended temporal effect was correctly reproduced, and the paper itself notes these metrics only partially capture perceptual and temporal nuances.

The V2V training data is generated by existing image/video generative models, so it may contain systematic artifacts and biases. The paper does not provide sufficient evidence that the synthesized paired videos reliably isolate the effect from content and motion, which could limit the model's learned disentanglement.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code is promised upon publication, but dataset release details are unclear, and training uses LoRA fine-tuning of a 14B model for only 10K steps, making it uncertain how well the results would reproduce with the full proposed dataset.

The architecture is a fairly direct extension of channel concatenation and conditioning masks. The paper does not ablate key design choices, such as cross-attention versus channel concatenation, reference-token handling, or the effect of each data source. Some architecture details are deferred to the supplement, and the description of reference-latent merging is somewhat confusing.

The method doubles inference cost due to dual conditioning (about 7 minutes per video vs. 3.5 minutes for baselines), which may limit practical impact; the 'tuning-free' framing is also slightly misleading since the model is trained with LoRA adapters, even if no test-time optimization is required.

Ethical and broader societal implications are not discussed, despite the method enabling realistic video manipulations of people and effects. Given the task's potential for misuse, a discussion of safeguards, consent, and dataset licensing would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Introduces a new and well-motivated task, reference-video-based temporal visual effect transfer, and provides a large-scale triplet dataset with over 120K triplets and 1,700+ effect categories.

The data construction pipeline is a substantial contribution: it combines LoRA-based image-to-video effects, an automated video-to-video generation pipeline with pose and first/last-frame conditioning, and programmatic temporal effects for scalable supervision.

The method extends a recent strong video diffusion backbone to jointly condition on input video, reference effect video, and text, and demonstrates feed-forward inference without per-effect test-time optimization.
Qualitative comparisons show clear advantages over text-only, depth/pose-conditioned, and text-based video editing baselines in reproducing time-varying effects while preserving input content.
The human study is extensive by current standards: 2AFC comparisons across multiple dimensions, over 15K annotations from 500+ annotators, and consistent win rates above chance for RVA, IVA, and OM.
The paper evaluates generalization to unseen LoRA effects and unseen programmatic effect hyperparameters/prompts, which supports the claim of generalizing beyond training effect categories.
Controllable guidance interpolation between reference and input adherence is a practically useful addition for real video editing applications.
The limitations section honestly discusses occlusion failures, human-centric data bias, and doubled inference cost.
weaknesses: The title and abstract emphasize a "tuning-free" framework, but the model is fine-tuned with LoRA on a 14B video diffusion backbone for 10K steps. It is tuning-free only at inference, not during training, which may mislead readers about the method's cost and nature.

The evaluation lacks ground-truth paired validation data. Reference and input similarities via CLIP/VideoPrism are weak proxies: higher reference similarity can reflect content/motion copying rather than transfer of the effect itself, and the paper does not provide a metric that disentangles effect from reference content.

User-study win rates are mostly 57–67% over baselines. While statistically above chance, the margins are modest and could be sensitive to baseline prompting, task framing, or the specific validation effects chosen. The IVA result against the no-reference ablation is near chance (51.3%), as expected, but it underscores that gains on some dimensions are small.

Baselines omit reference-based video editing, video personalization, and style-transfer methods adapted to the reference-video setting. The comparison is mainly against text-, depth-, or pose-conditioned models, which cannot use the reference video and thus makes the advantage somewhat expected.

The dataset is a central contribution, but the paper only promises code release and does not clearly commit to releasing the dataset, prompts, splits, or model checkpoints. Reproducibility and benchmark value are therefore limited.

The automated V2V data pipeline uses synthetic image/video generators and GPT-4o-generated prompts. The resulting triplets may contain generator artifacts and stylistic biases; no quantitative analysis of training-data quality, diversity, or effect alignment is provided.

Architecture and implementation details are sparse: there is no clear explanation of how reference and input videos of different lengths are aligned, how reference latents are temporally resampled, how positional encodings handle the doubled token sequence, or how conditioning dropout is scheduled.

Supplemental quantitative results show lower dynamic degree than several baselines in some settings (e.g., 0.143 vs 0.190 for code-based V2V and 0.711 vs 0.816 for I2V), which may indicate weaker transfer of dynamic effects. This is not analyzed in the main text.

The claim that the model disentangles the reference effect from reference content/motion is not directly tested. Since the reference is a full video with strong content and motion cues, the model may partly copy reference-specific content, especially in ambiguous effects.

There is no broader societal-impact discussion of realistic video effect transfer, including potential misuse for deepfakes, non-consensual manipulation, or misinformation, despite the human-centric and identity-transforming nature of many effects.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely novel and challenging task: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video onto an input image/video while preserving input content and motion. This reference-video-effect transfer formulation is a useful extension beyond text-only or static-reference video editing.

The proposed dataset is a substantial contribution in scope: over 120K triplets and roughly 1,700 effects built from LoRA-based I2V effects, a scalable V2V generation pipeline, and programmatic temporal effects. If truly released and validated, it could enable future work.

The model design reasonably extends an existing strong backbone (Wan2.1 FLF2V) by adding joint conditioning on input video, reference effect video, and text, with mask-based conditioning and multi-directional classifier-free guidance for controlling adherence.

Qualitative examples in Figures 6-8 demonstrate plausible transfer of effects such as camera motion, lighting changes, and character transformations, and the method is shown in a feed-forward inference regime without per-video optimization.

The human study is relatively extensive in annotation count (over 15K annotations, 500+ annotators) and evaluates multiple dimensions (reference adherence, input adherence, overall match), which is appropriate for a perceptual task.
The paper includes a limitations section acknowledging occlusion failures, human-centric dataset bias, and doubled inference cost due to dual conditioning.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks direct ground-truth effect-transfer validation. Even for code-based effects, where ground-truth outputs could be computed by applying the same programmatic effect to the input video, the paper does not report such comparisons. Instead, it relies on embedding-similarity proxies and user preference, which can reward copying reference content or appearance rather than transferring temporal dynamics.

The user study results are only modestly above chance, with win rates around 57-67%. More concerning, the No Ref ablation is close to the full method on reference adherence (e.g., 56.8% in I2V and 57.5% in V2V), suggesting that reference conditioning provides only limited benefit or that the study is underpowered. No confidence intervals are reported, only bootstrap standard deviations, and the total number of forced-choice comparisons per experiment is unclear.

The baselines are not reference-conditioned and therefore cannot access the reference effect video; they only receive text prompts. This makes the main comparison unfair and does not establish that RefVFX outperforms reference-based alternatives. The paper also does not empirically compare against relevant reference-based video customization/style/personalization methods (e.g., IP-Adapter variants, VideoAlchemy, Dynamic Concepts, ConceptMaster), despite discussing them in related work.

The technical novelty is limited. The method largely fine-tunes an existing Wan2.1 model with LoRA and concatenates reference latents. There is no explicit mechanism for disentangling the temporal effect from the reference video's content and motion, which is central to the claimed task. The 'tuning-free' framing is also somewhat misleading because the approach requires large-scale fine-tuning and a new conditioning scheme.

Dataset quality and validity are not sufficiently established. LoRA-based data essentially distills existing LoRA effects; the custom V2V pipeline depends on chained image/video generation and editing models that may introduce appearance/motion inconsistencies; and code-based effects are mostly simple programmatic filters. The paper does not quantify training-pair quality, failure rates, or dataset biases, nor does it discuss licensing, consent, or privacy for human-centric source data.

Quantitative results do not strongly support the claims. Tables 3 and 4 show only small margins in reference similarity, with lower input similarity or first-frame similarity in some settings relative to baselines. VBench results in Table 10 show lower dynamic degree and sometimes lower aesthetic/motion scores, yet the paper characterizes performance as comparable or superior. This weakens the case that the method transfers effects without harming video quality.

The ablation study is thin. It only drops reference conditioning in the user study, without systematic ablations on architecture, mask design, condition dropout, guidance, data mixture, or effect disentanglement. Reproducibility details such as LoRA rank, learning rate, exact text prompts, training splits, and dataset release plans are insufficient.

The paper does not discuss broader societal risks, such as non-consensual identity manipulation, face/body transformations, or misinformation, which are particularly relevant for a method that transfers effects onto arbitrary videos and is trained partly on human-centric data.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically important task: transferring a temporally evolving visual effect from a reference video to a target image/video, which is difficult to specify via text, keyframes, or static reference images. The paper provides a systematic first study and dataset for this reference-video-to-video effect transfer problem.

Introduces a large-scale dataset of over 120K triplets and 1,700 distinct effects built from three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V effects, a scalable V2V pipeline, and programmatic effects). This dataset and benchmark could be a lasting contribution to the community.

Provides a clear conditioning architecture on top of strong video diffusion backbones: the model jointly conditions on reference effect latents, input video latents, and text, with hybrid masks and multi-directional classifier-free guidance to control reference/input adherence.

Includes a substantial human preference study with over 15K annotations across neural V2V, I2V, and code-based V2V settings, plus comparisons to strong baselines and a No-Ref ablation. Qualitative results demonstrate generalization to unseen effects and improved temporal alignment over prompt-only baselines.
The paper is generally well-structured and includes useful appendix material on dataset composition, effect types, hyperparameters, limitations, and additional VBench-style metrics.
weaknesses: The paper is marketed as 'tuning-free,' but it fine-tunes a 14B-parameter Wan2.1 FLF2V model with LoRAs. While this may mean no per-effect optimization at inference time, the phrasing is misleading and should be clarified as 'no test-time optimization' rather than 'tuning-free.'

The dataset triplet formulation in Section 3.2 contains a notational error: it selects two distinct pairs but then writes the same indices for both pairs, and the constructed triplet appears to reuse the same output as reference and target. This obscures exactly how triplets are formed and should be corrected.

The quantitative evaluation lacks ground-truth triplets, so the reported VideoPrism/CLIP similarities are proxy metrics rather than measures of effect-transfer success. Human win rates are often only modestly above chance (e.g., 53.7% ± 2.2 for IVA vs. VACE Pose), and the claim of 'large user preference' overstates the observed margins. Significance tests and effect sizes should be reported.

Baselines are not reference-conditioned and cannot directly consume the reference effect video, so for Reference Video Adherence they are at a structural disadvantage. The No-Ref ablation helps, but stronger reference-conditioned or adapted baselines (e.g., cross-attention or concept-personalization methods) would make the comparison more convincing.

The dataset is largely synthetic and human-centric: the V2V pipeline relies on generated images, first-last-frame interpolation, and pose conditioning; the code-based effects are often simple programmatic filters/transitions rather than the complex cinematic effects claimed. There is little quantitative validation of training triplet alignment or artifact rates, which may limit real-world generalization.

Architectural novelty is limited: the core conditioning mechanism appears to be latent concatenation plus LoRA fine-tuning of an existing model. There is no ablation on the conditioning design, data mixture, or scaling behavior, so it is unclear how much the dataset versus the architecture drives performance.

Inference is expensive, roughly doubling token count and taking about 7 minutes per video on an A100. This is acknowledged as a limitation but is not addressed, and the efficiency claim relative to baselines is weak.

Reproducibility is not yet ensured: the code and dataset are only promised, and key details such as filtering criteria, pairing validation, and exact training configurations are either missing or relegated to an unspecified supplement. The absence of a deeper societal-impact discussion is also notable given the potential for realistic video manipulation.
